title: I want 10 properties in 10 years on RM5,500 a month. Too aggressive?
excerpt: A 29-year-old with RM50,000 saved wants positive cash flow and ten properties within 15 years. Sean explains cash back against cash flow, how rent drives a high-rise's value, and why he should go slowly.

qa.asker: YK, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: YK is 29, works in a helping profession and earns about RM5,500 a month. He has a six-month emergency fund, RM50,000 in savings and comprehensive insurance, and recently joined a bulk-purchase club. He wants positive cash flow and early retirement, and is weighing a completed unit with high cash back but a monthly shortfall, then two more units soon after.
qa.question: Should he take high cash back with negative cash flow, how is capital growth judged, is buying three units in quick succession overcommitting, and should spare cash go into a flexi loan?
qa.quote: So, my suggestion is to go slow.
qa.answer: Take positive cash flow over cash back if he can, buy one unit at a time and get each one rented before the next, and build his salary first. Ten properties in ten years on RM5,500 a month is a target nobody is holding him to.

reasons.title: Cash back is borrowed money
reasons.body: It suits someone using it to clear credit card debt at about 18% or a personal loan at about 8%, or a business owner using a flexi loan as cheap working capital. Without that need, a smaller loan with rent above the instalment is better; buyers who spent their cash back are the ones who ended up in auctions.

reasons.title: Rent sets a high-rise's value
reasons.body: Each RM450 a month of surplus rent supports about RM100,000 more loan over 35 years at 4%. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought for about RM950,000, rents for about RM1,500 above its instalment, so the next investor could pay about RM1.25 million and still break even. That surplus mostly happens in tier one locations.

reasons.title: Studios suit only expensive land
reasons.body: Studios work where land is too costly for bigger units, such as Mont Kiara, Bangsar South and KLCC. In outlying areas they are a mismatch, however cheap they look.

reasons.title: Active income drives the portfolio
reasons.body: Investors who build portfolios fast usually earn RM30,000 or more. On RM5,500, a RM20,000 repair can hurt. Property keeps you rich; growing income is what makes you rich, and rental income replacing a salary is a goal for 55 or 60, not 35.

actions: Choose a lower loan with positive cash flow over cash back you don't need.
Rent each unit out before committing to the next.
Pick one route, subsale, auction or bulk purchase, and execute it rather than joining several courses.
Put spare cash in a flexi loan unless you can reliably earn more than the loan's 3.8% to 4%.
Set a goal by monthly cash flow or total value, not a number of units by a deadline.
qa.caveat: For someone with expensive debts to clear, a high cash back unit with a small monthly shortfall can make sense, provided the cash back is kept as a buffer and not spent.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #284. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in May 2025. Sean is a client of FAR Capital, the bulk-purchase club YK has joined, not its owner; he says he bought his last four properties through it at members' prices. He leaves the specific project YK is considering to the club's advisers.
